info: Rhododendrons are popular, colorful spring flowers, famous for their beautiful blooms.
They are low maintenance.
Rhododendrons are evergreen or deciduous shrubs.
They get big — up to 20 feet tall and 15 feet wide.
They are toxic to humans, pets, and livestock.
history: Rhododendrons date back over 55 million years.
Their recorded human history spans ancient honey mishaps and 19th-century plant hunting.

info: Showy in pollinator gardens.
Blooms blue in late spring.
Has a shrubby appearance — forms a bushy mound with blue-green, clover-like leaves.
Host plant for six butterfly species, including the wild indigo duskywing.
Attractive black seed pods that rattle in the wind.
Named "false indigo" because colonial settlers used it to make a blue dye that was weaker than true indigo.
Fixes nitrogen in the soil — it belongs to the pea family.
care: Flowers best in full sun.
Can take several years to reach full height — 3 to 4 years to reach full size.
Deep taproot makes it drought tolerant over time, and deer resistant once established.
Choose the permanent spot carefully — the long taproot means it dislikes being moved.
From seed, the hard seed coat needs scarification (sandpaper or an overnight warm-water soak).
Almost no maintenance once established. Stems die back to the ground in winter.
plants.warning: Contains toxic alkaloids — do not eat any part of this plant.

info: A yellow, daisy-like flower.
It attracts bees, butterflies, and other pollinators.
The tickseed is a low-maintenance wildflower.
Why is it called "tickseed"? The name comes from the flower's seeds — they look like ticks. But the tickseed does not attract ticks.
care: Sunlight: at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sun for the best blooms.
Soil: well-drained, lean, or sandy. It tolerates poor soil.
Water: an adult tickseed needs only about one inch of water a week. Seedlings need consistent watering until their roots take hold.
Height depends on the variety — a regular tickseed is around 3 feet, a dwarf can be as short as 8 inches, and a tall one can grow taller still.

info: Height: 1 to 4 feet tall.
Foliage: leaves are rough and hairy, growing up to six inches.
Plant type depends on how it is treated — that determines how long it will live.
It self-seeds.
Highly drought tolerant and adaptable.
Thrives in sun.
care: Plant them in full sun so they get at least six hours of sun.
Use loose, well-draining soil — they dislike sitting in soggy soil.
Water plants regularly during the growing season.

info: The woodland strawberry (Fragaria vesca) is a flower in the rose family.
It occurs naturally across the Northern Hemisphere.
It is also known as the wild strawberry and the wood strawberry.
It has dark green leaves and bright red fruits.
The fruits are small yet flavorful.

info: Virginia spiderwort is edible, but parts of it are poisonous.
The flowers come in three colors: blue, pink, or white.
They grow and thrive in moist woods, stream banks, clearings, and roadsides.
Spiderwort is native to the eastern and east-central regions of North America.
care: Water: keep the soil moist, and water deeply if it is dry — about 1 inch per week.
Avoid soggy soil. Make sure the plant drains well.
Give it partial shade, about 4 to 6 hours a day.
Good drainage matters.
If the soil is healthy, fertilizer will rarely be needed.
Prune to prevent a floppy look.

info: It handles extreme summer heat, drought, and even road salt with ease once established.
It won Plant of the Year in 1992 from the Perennial Plant Association.
It is native to the southern USA — states such as Florida and Texas.
care: Low maintenance.
Thrives best in full sun, 6 to 8 hours every day.
Handles poor, rocky, or sandy soil.
1 inch of water every week.
Little to no fertilizer needed.
Needs good soil drainage.
Wet or soggy soil harms the plant. Water regularly until the roots take hold.

info: Sunchokes are resilient, high-yielding perennial sunflowers native to North America.
The above-ground plant looks like a wild sunflower and easily grows 6 to 14 feet tall — tall enough to shade nearby crops.
They spread rapidly through underground rhizomes. Any tiny piece of tuber left in the soil grows into a new plant next spring.
The edible parts are the knobby underground tubers, which look like ginger root. One plant can yield over a gallon of tubers.
They need a long season — 120 to 150 days — and bloom bright yellow late, in August or September.
They store energy as inulin, not starch. Gut bacteria love it, which is why sunchokes are famous for causing gas.
Frost makes them sweeter: it breaks inulin down into fructose for a nuttier flavor.
Raw, they are crisp and sweet like water chestnuts. Cooked, they turn creamy like a potato.
care: Plant in a 5- to 15-gallon container or heavy grow bag — never straight into a greenhouse bed, or they will take over.
Use a loose, well-draining mix of potting soil, compost, and a little sand or perlite.
Plant tubers 3 to 5 inches deep with the eyes facing up, spaced about 12 inches apart.
Water thoroughly after planting, then mulch 3 inches deep with straw or leaves.
Fall: keep the greenhouse ventilated. They like 65–90°F. Water when the top 2 inches are dry — never waterlogged.
Winter: do not heat the greenhouse. They need a real chill to break dormancy and sweeten. Water the bare minimum.
Late winter: as daylight grows, shoots appear. Increase watering once they do.
Spring: after the last frost, move containers outside to full sun — they will outgrow the greenhouse ceiling.

info: Formerly known as Aster novae-angliae.
It blooms late — one of the last big nectar sources before frost.
It needs at least 6 to 8 hours of direct sunlight each day to grow and bloom its best.
care: Sunlight: prefers full sun, though it tolerates light partial shade.
Soil: adapts to clay, loam, or sandy soil, but prefers rich, moist, well-draining conditions.
Water: needs medium to moist soil. It tolerates short dry spells once established.
Pinch back the stems 1 to 2 inches in late spring so the plant grows bushier and is less likely to flop over.
Plant it behind shorter perennials — the lower leaves brown and drop by flowering time.
Space plants 1 to 2 feet apart for airflow, to prevent fungal leaf diseases.
Divide large clumps every 2 to 3 years in spring to keep the plant vigorous.
